thesis: Whether taking part in the African slave trade is morally lawful (Newton's Authentic Narrative, written 1762-63 about his years as a slave-ship captain, says that while engaged in the trade he 'never had the least scruple as to its lawfulness'; his 1788 Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade makes a public confession that he was once 'an active instrument, in a business at which my heart now shudders').

early.text: During the time I was engaged in the slave trade, I never had the least scruple as to its lawfulness. I was, upon the whole, satisfied with it, as the appointment Providence had marked out for me ; yet it was, in many respects, far from eligible. It is, indeed, accounted a genteel employment, and is usually very profitable, though to me it did not prove so, the Lord seeing that a large increase of wealth could not be good for me.

Haweis written 1762-63, first published 1764), text as reprinted in The Works of the Rev. John Newton (1846 reprint; archive.org OCR 'worksofrevjohnne00newt', cleaned copy)

announced.text: If my testimony should not be necessary, or serviceable, yet, perhaps, I am bound, in conscience, to take shame to myself by a public confession, which, however sincere, comes too late to prevent, or repair, the misery and mischief to which I have, formerly, been accessary. I hope it will always be a subject of humiliating reflection to me, that I was, once, an active instrument, in a business at which my heart now shudders.
announced.work: Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (London, 1788; Project Gutenberg #68056)
announced.locator: Opening of the pamphlet: end of the paragraph beginning 'If I attempt, after what has been done' and the start of the next paragraph, 'I hope it will always be a subject of humiliating reflection to me'

unannounced.text: Though unwilling to give offence to a single person; in such a cause, I ought not to be afraid of offending many, by declaring the truth; if, indeed, there can be many, whom even interest can prevail upon to contradict the common sense of mankind, by pleading for a commerce, so iniquitous, so cruel, so oppressive, so destructive, as the African Slave Trade!
unannounced.work: Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (London, 1788; Project Gutenberg #68056)
unannounced.locator: Closing paragraph of the pamphlet, just before 'FINIS'

But within these two or three years I have accustomed myself chiefly to writing, and have not found time to read many books besides the scriptures.

thesis: Whether Christ was a mere man and Christianity a Unitarian religion of natural theology whose chief doctrine is immortality 'proved to us by the resurrection of Jesus' (Coleridge's 1795 Addresses to the People), or the incarnate God of Trinitarian doctrine (Biographia Literaria, 1817, where he calls his Unitarian opinions 'in many and most important points erroneous' and says Unitarianism and the Trinitarian faith are opposites).

early.text: And truly, the most exalted forms of society are cemented and preserved by the purest notions of religion. But whatever I may deem of the justice of their Lordship's observations, the prudence and policy of them have gained my immediate assent. Alas ! what room would there be for bishops or for priests in a religion where deity is the only object of reverence, and our immortality the only article of faith — immortality made probable to us by the light of nature, and proved to us by the resurrection of Jesus.
early.work: Conciones ad Populum, or Addresses to the People (Bristol, February 1795; preface dated Nov 1795), as reprinted with The Plot Discovered (1795) in Essays on His Own Times, vol. I (1850; archive.org OCR 'essaysonhisownti01coleuoft', cleaned copy)
early.locator: 'On the Present War' (second address), long footnote on bishops, Unitarians and the resurrection of Jesus

announced.text: For I was at that time and long after, though a Trinitarian (that is ad normam Platonis) in philosophy, yet a zealous Unitarian in religion; more accurately, I was a Psilanthropist, one of those who believe our Lord to have been the real son of Joseph, and who lay the main stress on the resurrection rather than on the crucifixion. O! never can I remember those days with either shame or regret. For I was most sincere, most disinterested. My opinions were indeed in many and most important points erroneous; but my heart was single.
announced.locator: Chapter X, account of his preaching tour for The Watchman, 'a zealous Unitarian in religion'

unannounced.text: But this I have said, and shall continue to say: that if the doctrines, the sum of which I believe to constitute the truth in Christ, be Christianity, then Unitarianism is not, and vice versa: and that, in speaking theologically and impersonally, i.e. of Psilanthropism and Theanthropism as schemes of belief, without reference to individuals, who profess either the one or the other, it will be absurd to use a different language as long as it is the dictate of common sense, that two opposites cannot properly be called by the same name.
unannounced.locator: Chapter XXIV (Conclusion), paragraph on the Unitarians, Psilanthropism and Theanthropism

control.text: But even these means have proved insufficient ; and the poor wretches, whom hunger had driven or artifice seduced into the deeds of death, have fallen so fast, that crimping has been found necessary. The Irish* Regiment, recently landed at Pill near this city is a melancholy instance — By long confinement and by filth they have almost ceased to resemble men.

thesis: Whether the six days of creation in Genesis were natural days of twenty-four hours, with the geological ages lying in a gap before them (the Chalmers-Buckland scheme that Miller defended in 1847), or vast 'prophetic' periods of immense length (the view of his Testimony of the Rocks, where he says he 'certainly did once believe with Chalmers and with Buckland that the six days were simply natural days').

early.text: Now, let it be admitted, for the argument's sake, that the earth existed in the dark and void state described here only six days, of twenty-four hours each, before the creation of man ; and that the going forth of the Spirit and the breaking out of the light, on this occasion, were events immediately introductory to the creation to which we ourselves belong. And what then ? It is evident, from the continuity of the narrative in the passage, say the anti-geologists, that there could have been no creations on this earth prior to the present one. Nay, not so : for aught that appears in the narrative, there might have been many.
early.work: First Impressions of England and Its People (1847; 1856 American printing; archive.org OCR 'firstimpressions00milluoft', cleaned copy)
early.locator: Chapter XVII ('Cowper and the Geologists'), about p. 345 of the 1856 printing: reply to the anti-geologists on the opening verses of Genesis

announced.text: It will be seen that I adopt, in my Third and Fourth Lectures, that scheme of reconciliation between the Geologic and Mosaic Records which accepts the six days of creation as vastly extended periods; and I have been reminded by a somewhat captious critic that I once held a very different view, and twitted with what he terms inconsistency. I certainly did once believe with Chalmers and with Buckland that the six days were simply natural days of twenty-four hours each,--that they had compressed the entire work of the existing creation,--and that the latest of the geologic ages was separated by a great chaotic gap from our own.
announced.work: The Testimony of the Rocks (written 1856, published 1857; Project Gutenberg #28248; Miller's preface and twelve lectures only, cleaned selection)
announced.locator: Preface ('To the Reader'), paragraph on the Third and Fourth Lectures

unannounced.text: The days must have been prophetic days, introduced, indeed, into the panorama of creation as mayhap mere openings and droppings of the curtain, but not the less symbolic of that series of successive periods, each characterized by its own productions and events, in which creation itself was comprised.
unannounced.work: The Testimony of the Rocks (written 1856, published 1857; Project Gutenberg #28248; Miller's preface and twelve lectures only, cleaned selection)
unannounced.locator: Lecture Fourth (the Mosaic vision of creation), paragraph on the prophetic days

thesis: Whether Rubens deserves 'the most reverential' admiration (Modern Painters vol. I, 1843: 'I never will speak of Rubens but with the most reverential feeling') or is to be seen as a vulgar, profane painter (Ruskin's 1860 preface to vol. V regrets 'the strong expressions of admiration for Rubens' in the first volume, blames a 'boy's veneration for Rubens' physical art-power', and in vol. V he treats him as a painter who 'performs' rather than worships).

early.text: I never have spoken, and I never will speak of Rubens but with the most reverential feeling; and whatever imperfections in his art may have resulted from his unfortunate want of seriousness and incapability of true passion, his calibre of mind was originally such that I believe the world may see another Titian and another Raffaelle, before it sees another Rubens.

early.locator: Part II, Section I, Chapter II 'Of Truth of Color', discussion of the Dulwich landscape attributed to Rubens

announced.text: At that time I had seen much of nature, and had been several times in Italy, wintering once in Rome; but had chiefly delighted in northern art, beginning, when a mere boy, with Rubens and Rembrandt. It was long before I got quit of a boy's veneration for Rubens' physical art-power; and the reader will, perhaps, on this ground forgive the strong expressions of admiration for Rubens, which, to my great regret, occur in the first volume.
announced.work: Modern Painters, vol. V (1860), Preface (Library Edition text, Project Gutenberg #44329)
announced.locator: Preface, paragraph beginning 'The first volume was the expansion of a reply to a magazine article' (second half)

unannounced.text: Rubens has also painted himself and his family in an equally elaborate piece. But they are not _worshipping_ the Madonna. They are _performing_ the Madonna, and her saintly entourage.
unannounced.work: Modern Painters, vol. V (1860), Preface (Library Edition text, Project Gutenberg #44329)
unannounced.locator: Part VIII ('Of Invention Formal'), Chapter VI 'Rubens and Cuyp'

control.text: I shall enter upon the examination of what is true in sky at greater length, because it is the only part of a picture of which all, if they will, may be competent judges. What I may have to assert respecting the rocks of Salvator, or the boughs of Claude, I can scarcely prove, except to those whom I can immure for a month or two in the fastnesses of the Apennines, or guide in their summer walks again and again through the ravines of Sorrento. But what I say of the sky can be brought to an immediate test by all, and I write the more decisively, in the hope that it may be so.
control.work: Modern Painters, vol. I (1843; Library Edition text, Project Gutenberg #29907)

thesis: Whether the totem is the receptacle of the external soul of the person who claims it, so that the savage's life is bound up with a particular animal or plant of the totem species (Frazer's Golden Bough, 1890: 'The totem, if I am right, is simply the receptacle in which a man keeps his life'; in Totemism and Exogamy, 1910, he writes only that on such facts he 'formerly based a theory' of the external soul and has since adopted other views of totemism).

early.text: Now if the relations are similar, the explanation which holds good of the one ought equally to hold good of the other. Therefore the reason why a tribe revere a particular species of animals or plants (for the tribal totem may be a plant) and call themselves after it, must be a belief that the life of each individual of the tribe is bound up with some one animal or plant of the species, and that his or her death would be the consequence of killing that particular animal, or destroying that particular plant.
early.work: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, vol. II (first edition, 1890; archive.org OCR 'b21904455', cleaned copy)
early.locator: Chapter IV, section 4 'The external soul in folk-custom', passage on sex-totems and totemism (vol. II p. 337), paragraph beginning 'But when a savage names himself after an animal'

announced.text: His or her life is apparently thought to be so bound up with that of the animal that an injury done to the animal injures correspondingly the man or woman, while its destruction entails his or her death. On these and similar facts I formerly based a theory that a totem may have been supposed to contain the external soul of the person who claimed it.
announced.work: Totemism and Exogamy, vol. I (1910), 'An Ethnographical Survey of Totemism' (archive.org OCR 'totemismexogamyt01fraz', cleaned copy)
announced.locator: Chapter II (Totemism in South-Eastern Australia), the Wotjobaluk

unannounced.text: This idea of spirit individuals associated with churinga and resident at certain definite spots lies at the root of the present totemic system of the Arunta and kindred tribes. For the natives believe that every living member of the tribe is the reincarnation of one of these spirits.
unannounced.work: Totemism and Exogamy, vol. I (1910), 'An Ethnographical Survey of Totemism' (archive.org OCR 'totemismexogamyt01fraz', cleaned copy)
unannounced.locator: Chapter I (Totemism in Central Australia), the Arunta

This introduces us to a new aspect of the corn-spirit, which we must now examine. By doing so we shall not onlyhave fresh examples of killing the god, but may hope also to clear up some points which remain obscure in the myths and worship of Attis, Adonis, Osiris, Dionysus, Demeter, and Virbius.

thesis: Whether political power should rest on persons (universal representation, the suffrage of every individual, no property qualification for legislators, as in Wordsworth's republican Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff, 1793) or on property and the existing complex system of representation (his 1821 Letter to a Friend: 'When I was young ... I thought it derogatory to human nature to set up property in preference to person as a title for legislative power. That notion has vanished.'; in 1831 he defends the English constitution against Reform).

early.text: But, to resume the subject of universal representation, I ought to have mentioned before, that in the choice of its representatives a people will not immorally hold out wealth as a criterion of integrity, nor lay down as a fundamental rule, that to be qualified for the trying duties of legislation a citizen should be possessed of a certain fixed property. Virtues, talents, and acquirements are all that it will look for.
early.work: Apology for the French Revolution: A Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff (1793; unpublished in his lifetime, printed in Grosart's Prose Works of William Wordsworth, 1876; Project Gutenberg #16550)
early.locator: Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff, section on universal representation (Gutenberg lines 1542-1548)

announced.text: I should think that I had lived to little purpose if my notions on the subject of government had undergone no modification: my youth must, in that case, have been without enthusiasm, and my manhood endued with small capability of profiting by reflection.
announced.work: Letters and extracts from letters, in Grosart's Prose Works of William Wordsworth, vol. III (1876); passage from the Letter to a Friend, Rydal Mount, 4 Dec 1821; Project Gutenberg #16550
announced.locator: Letter to a Friend, 4 Dec 1821 ('Of alleged Changes in Political Opinions'), second paragraph of Wordsworth's reply

unannounced.text: The constitution of England, which seems about to be destroyed, offers to my mind the sublimest contemplation which the history of society and government have ever presented to it; and for this cause especially, that its principles have the character of preconceived ideas, archetypes of the pure intellect, while they are, in fact, the results of a humble-minded experience.
unannounced.work: Letters and extracts from letters, in Grosart's Prose Works of William Wordsworth, vol. III (1876); passage from the Letter to a Friend, Rydal Mount, 4 Dec 1821; Project Gutenberg #16550
unannounced.locator: Letter to Professor Hamilton, Dublin, 22 Nov 1831, on the Reform Bill

control.text: I have spoken of laws partial and oppressive; our penal code is so crowded with disproportioned penalties and indiscriminate severity that a conscientious man would sacrifice, in many instances, his respect for the laws to the common feelings of humanity; and there must be a strange vice in that legislation from which can proceed laws in whose execution a man cannot be instrumental without forfeiting his self-esteem and incurring the contempt of his fellow-citizens.
control.work: Apology for the French Revolution: A Letter to the Bishop of Llandaff (1793; unpublished in his lifetime, printed in Grosart's Prose Works of William Wordsworth, 1876; Project Gutenberg #16550)
